title: CopilotKit/OpenBot — Open-source AI coworkers that each get a computer of their own: a browser, files and tools, with every action decided before it happens and recorded after. Bring any AG-UI agent.
content:
The AI assistant your company can actually own. Same shape as ChatGPT, Claude or Grok, with one difference that matters: it runs on your infrastructure and you can change anything about it. Any agent stack, through AG-UI.
Each coworker gets a computer of its own: a real browser with its own logins, its own files, and only the tools you grant. Every action decided before it happens and recorded after.
Talk to an engineer · Have us build it with you · copilotkit.ai/openbot · Quick start · Docs
demo-openbot.mp4
Bring any AG-UI agent, written on a framework or by hand, and it arrives as a coworker with a channel of its own. Watch it work on its own screen, take the wheel when it reaches something it should not do alone, then hand it back. It answers with components rather than only prose, and the whole thing runs on your own machine.
A template, not a product. OpenBot is meant to be cloned and made your own. There is no hosted version to sign up for, and nothing here is published as a package to depend on: every workspace in this repository is private. You take the repository, replace the example tenant package under examples/ with your own coworkers, channels and skills, and run it. Everything below describes a starting point, not a finished thing somebody operates for you.
Alpha, and under active development. OpenBot is early. Expect rough edges and bugs, and expect things to move. Issues and pull requests are welcome.
Runs on your machine. Everything below is written for a laptop. .env.example carries OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true, which admits every request as one administrator, so a fresh clone reaches the product without registering an OAuth client first. Sign-in turns that off, and is required before anybody else can reach the deployment.
We can build this for you, or with you, at your company. Our engineers will stand OpenBot up inside your infrastructure, customize it into something that looks like your own product, and hand it back to you to keep changing. Start the conversation.
In the meantime, run all of it on your laptop, Intelligence included: CopilotKit's free Developer plan covers running Intelligence locally in Docker on a Mac.
An agent platform that runs inside your own infrastructure. Docker Compose brings up every part of it, the data sits in your PostgreSQL, and the model is yours to choose: no model ships in the box, and an administrator supplies the credential, which is encrypted at rest and never logged.
A deployment starts with two coworkers, and they are configuration rather than code: General Assistant for everyday work and Knowledge for company questions. A Risk Analyst joins them once its endpoint is configured, and ten more wait in examples/fintech/catalog/, each doing one job — reading an expense claim against the policy as written, turning a meeting note into the follow-ups actually in it, drafting release notes from what shipped, triaging a ticket, answering a new starter from the handbook, writing a brief that names what it could not find, writing up an interview, handing an on-call shift over, assembling what is known before a renewal, and grouping customer feedback into themes it can cite. Copy one into examples/fintech/agents/ to add it, write your own there or in agents.yaml, or make one from /bots in the UI.
Anything a Bot does to a computer, a file, an MCP server or a component goes through one gateway that decides and records it. That is the difference between an agent that can use your tools and an agent you can let near them.
More at copilotkit.ai/openbot.
A Bot is any endpoint speaking AG-UI, the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework.
- Docker, for PostgreSQL and the shipped Bots.
- Bun 1.3+, for the app and API server.
- A CopilotKit Intelligence project and license. A free plan is available, and Intelligence can be self-hosted.
- A model key. The proof-of-concept Bot uses OpenAI; the LangGraph Bot can use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google.
Setting up with an AI assistant? Paste prompt.txt into it first. It carries the
same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in
.env.example are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start
script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against
this repository.
- Create .env:
cp .env.example .env bun install
- Connect a fresh managed Intelligence project: npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select
bun scripts/setup-learning.ts The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its
openbot Learning container, then writes both settings to .env. It preserves
custom container assignments and never replaces an existing OpenBot key; with one
set, it only creates openbot in that key's project if it is missing.
For fresh self-hosted setup, set INTELLIGENCE_API_URL to that deployment's
HTTPS API origin (or http://localhost for a local one) and run the helper
without the two npx commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for
your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. It writes
the API URL, the key and the container, not INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL, so
set that one to the same deployment yourself. Once openbot exists, the server assigns it
as the default by itself unless Admin → Automatic Learning
has a saved setting.
Managed Intelligence needs no separate licence token.
- Fill the remaining required values: 
  - OPENAI_API_KEY
Keep the managed Intelligence URLs from .env.example unless you run Intelligence yourself. The example KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is public and fine locally; generate your own with:
openssl rand -base64 32
- Run: bash scripts/start.sh
- Open http://localhost:3010.
scripts/start.sh starts Docker services, applies migrations, starts the API server on port 3001, starts the routine worker, starts the app on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps.
scripts/stop.sh takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; --keep-computers leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes.
To try Intelligence on one Mac instead of the managed service, follow
Evaluate Intelligence locally. The free
Developer plan qualifies. The local licence lasts 30 days and
npx copilotkit@latest local renew renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good
standing. It is a preview for macOS with Docker Desktop,
not a production installation. Run its
npx copilotkit@latest local connect from the OpenBot root, where .env is.
That command writes INTELLIGENCE_API_URL, INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL and
CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY to .env. OpenBot reads the first two as they are, but takes its project
key only from INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY and refuses to start without it, so copy the cpk-... value
across before bash scripts/start.sh:
INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY=cpk-...   # the value of CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY
To give the Bots a Learning container on that stack, see Automatic Learning.
One image carries the app, the API, the browser the Bots drive, and optionally PostgreSQL. Same
.env, no Kubernetes.
# The published image. Nothing to clone and nothing to build.
docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \
  -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql \
  ghcr.io/copilotkit/openbot:latest
# Or the tree you have in front of you.
docker build -t openbot .
docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \
  -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql openbot
Everything is on 3001 here, the app included, rather than the 3010 the clone uses. latest is the
most recent release and a version tag s

report.summary: CopilotKit's OpenBot is an open-source template for self-hosted AI coworkers, each with its own browser, files and tools, governed by a single action-deciding, recording gateway.
report.background: Enterprise interest in AI assistants has shifted from chat interfaces to agents that can actually do work: browse, read files, call APIs and use tools. But most capable assistants are hosted services, raising questions about data ownership, model choice and auditability. At the same time, the agent ecosystem is fragmented across frameworks such as LangGraph, CrewAI and Google ADK, making it hard to standardize governance. CopilotKit's OpenBot enters this gap as a cloneable, self-hosted template rather than a product. It leans on AG-UI, an open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so any compatible agent can become a coworker. The project is early alpha and explicitly aimed at teams that want to own the stack, customize the interface and keep every action on their own infrastructure.
key_points: Each AI coworker gets a dedicated computer: a real browser with its own logins, its own file space and only the tools an administrator grants. Every action passes through a single gateway that decides whether it is allowed before it happens and records it afterward, creating an auditable boundary between agents and company systems.

OpenBot is framework-agnostic because it speaks AG-UI, an open protocol for agent-to-user interaction. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or by hand all arrive the same way, so governance rides the protocol rather than any one vendor's stack.

The platform runs on your own infrastructure via Docker Compose, with data in your PostgreSQL and no model shipped in the box. An administrator supplies the model credential, which is encrypted at rest and never logged. Default coworkers such as General Assistant and Knowledge are configuration, not code, and more examples ship in the repo.

OpenBot is a template, not a hosted product: there is no sign-up, no published package to depend on and every workspace is private. Teams clone the repository, replace the example tenant package with their own coworkers, channels and skills, and run it. It is alpha, so rough edges and breaking changes are expected.

Getting started requires Docker, Bun 1.3+, a CopilotKit Intelligence project and license, and a model key. A start script brings up Docker services, runs migrations, starts the API and app, and checks health routes. A single container image is also available for simpler deployments.
report.impact: For the AI industry, OpenBot signals a shift toward governance-by-default and protocol-first agent infrastructure: instead of locking businesses into a hosted assistant, it treats permissions, audit trails and self-hosting as baseline features. For developers, it offers a framework-neutral way to turn existing agents into usable coworkers with screens, files and controlled tools, though the alpha status and operational setup mean real engineering effort. For regular users, the promise is a ChatGPT-like experience that runs on company infrastructure, with data staying in-house and sensitive actions gated by policy. It is unlikely to replace consumer assistants soon, but it gives enterprises a credible path to owned, auditable AI coworkers.
report.tools: Follow the CopilotKit/OpenBot repository and the AG-UI protocol specification. Related projects to watch or try include LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI and Google ADK for building agents, plus MCP for tool integration. Docker Compose and PostgreSQL are required for local deployment. The repo's prompt.txt is useful when setting up with an AI coding assistant.
